title: Rama and Sita in the Ramakien
source_ref: Ramakien, King Rama I's court version (completed c. 1798); Wat Phra Kaew murals; compared with Valmiki's Ramayana
paragraphs: The Ramakien is Thailand's telling of the Ramayana, completed at the court of King Rama I around 1798. Its hero is Phra Ram, an avatar of the god Narai, exiled to the forest with his wife Nang Sida and his brother Phra Lak, called Lakshmana in Sanskrit. Their quiet life ends when Thotsakan, the demon king of Longka, decides he must possess Sida.

Thotsakan sends the demon Marit to take the form of a golden deer. Sida begs her husband to catch it, and Rama and Lakshmana leave the hermitage. Alone, Sida is visited by Thotsakan disguised as a wandering ascetic. He seizes her and carries her through the sky to Longka. The vulture king Sadayu tries to stop him and is mortally wounded.

Rama gathers an army of monkeys. Hanuman, the white monkey son of the wind, leaps to Longka, finds Sida, and carries her ring back as proof. The monkeys build a causeway across the sea, and the war that follows fills many books with duels, disguises and losses. In the end Rama kills Thotsakan and Sida is freed.

The Thai version is not Valmiki's poem. Its tone is courtly and comic, Hanuman is a lover as well as a hero, and later books carry the story past the rescue into Sida's exile and the wars of her sons. The Ramakien is still performed as khon dance-drama, and its scenes line the galleries of Wat Phra Kaew in Bangkok.
notes: Thai retellings differ from Valmiki and from one another. The Ramakien expands Hanuman's adventures, names the demon king Thotsakan, and adds later books in which Sita is banished after a rakshasa tricks her into drawing Ravana's portrait. The 1798 date refers to King Rama I's court text; earlier Thai and Khmer versions circulated before it, and khon performances cut and rearrange episodes.

title: Hanuman and the Herbs
source_ref: Ramakien, the 'Hanuman Carries the Mountain' episode (King Rama I's version); Valmiki's Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda; Khmer Reamker
paragraphs: In the war for Longka, Thotsakan's son Intharachit strikes down Phra Lak with a magical arrow. Rama's brother lies unconscious, and the monkey army falls with him. The physician Chomphuphan says that the only cure grows on Mount Awut, far away, where a spinning weapon guards the herbs. Hanuman, son of the wind, volunteers to go.

Hanuman flies to the mountain, but the herbs are small and many, and he cannot tell which one will cure him. Rather than guess, he wrenches the whole mountain from the ground, hoists it onto his shoulder and carries it through the sky. The celestial guardians of the herbs watch, astonished, and follow him back to the battlefield.

The mountain will not sit on the island of Longka, so Hanuman carries it north until its fragrance reaches Phra Lak. The wounded brother and the fallen monkeys breathe the scent and wake. The guardians then take the mountain home. The episode is played for comedy as well as devotion: the mighty hero solves a delicate problem by lifting the entire landscape.

Thai and Khmer versions tell the errand differently. In the Ramakien the mountain is Mount Awut, guarded by a chakra and watched by devas; in Valmiki's Sanskrit poem Hanuman likewise cannot identify the herb and carries the mountain. The scene is among the most performed in Thai khon, where the flying monkey and the suspended mountain are a test of stagecraft.
notes: The episode appears in both the Ramakien and Valmiki's Ramayana, but the mountain's name, the herb's identity and the guardian figures vary. Thai performance tradition emphasises comedy and spectacle; Valmiki's account is shorter and more austere. The Khmer Reamker has its own version of the errand.

title: Dewi Sri and the Rice
source_ref: Wawacan Sulanjana (Sundanese, compiled 17th-19th century); Javanese and Balinese rice traditions; Balinese lontar and ritual practice
paragraphs: Dewi Sri is the rice goddess of Java and Bali. In the Sundanese telling, the gods are building a palace when the naga Anta, who has no hands, weeps. His tears become three jewelled eggs. One hatches into a beautiful girl, Nyai Pohaci Sanghyang Asri, and the gods raise her in heaven. Her beauty draws every eye, including the eye of her foster father, Batara Guru.

To prevent an incestuous scandal, the gods poison her. Storms punish them, and they bury her body far away on earth. From her grave grow the plants people need: coconut from her head, spices from her face, fruit from her breasts, bamboo from her thighs, tubers from her legs, and rice from her navel. In another version white rice grows from one eye and red rice from the other.

Rice is therefore not a commodity but a gift made from a goddess's body. Farmers honour Sri at planting and harvest. In Java, Sundanese communities hold the Seren Taun harvest rite and keep rice in the lumbung, the barn, where Sri is said to dwell. In Bali, small shrines in the fields and granaries are tended for Dewi Sri, and stylized cili figures associated with her appear in temple paintings and offerings.

The variants are real and local. Javanese, Sundanese and Balinese tellings give Sri different parents, different deaths and different companions; in Bali she is often paired with Sedana, and her image is carried in processions. Colonial and modern writers have sometimes flattened her into a single 'rice mother'. The rites, the offerings and the stories remain living practice, not a closed myth from the past.
notes: The story is told very differently in Java, Sunda and Bali. In the Sundanese Wawacan Sulanjana, Sri is poisoned by the gods and buried, and crops grow from her body; Balinese tradition pairs her with Sedana and honours her with particular offerings and shrines. Names, family relationships and ritual details vary by region, and the written texts were compiled centuries after the oral traditions.

title: The Naga of the Mekong
source_ref: Thai and Lao Mekong traditions of Phaya Naga; Khmer Preah Thong and Neang Neak foundation accounts; Thai press reporting on the Naga fireballs at Nong Khai
paragraphs: The naga is not a single monster but a class of serpent beings in the religious imagination of mainland Southeast Asia. In Theravada Buddhist cosmology they live beneath rivers, guard treasure and relics, and can take human form. Thai, Lao and Khmer traditions treat them as powerful, ambivalent and worthy of respect: guardians of water and land, and sometimes ancestors of ruling lines.

The Mekong is the naga's great home. Phaya Naga, the naga king, is said to live in the river's deep pools, and the naga is honoured wherever the river passes. In Khmer tradition the naga princess Neang Neak marries the Brahmin Preah Thong; her father, the naga king, drinks the water to reveal the land, and their union founds the kingdom.

At the end of Buddhist Lent, on the full moon of the eleventh lunar month, crowds gather at Nong Khai and on the Lao bank of the Mekong. Pink-red fireballs rise silently from the river into the night sky. Many believers say Phaya Naga sends them to celebrate the Buddha's return from heaven; scientists point to phosphine gas released from the riverbed. Both explanations are part of the event.

The naga is a living presence, not a folklore monster. Mekong towns hold boat races and fire-boat processions in its honour, temple stairways are carved as naga bodies, and offerings are left at the water. Thai, Lao and Khmer versions differ: the Lao naga is closely tied to the river and to the Lao kingdom, the Khmer naga to the founding of Funan, and the Thai Phaya Naga to Nong Khai and the fireballs.
notes: Naga traditions are living and locally variable, and the fireballs are contested. Believers and scientists explain them differently, and the number and timing of the sightings vary from year to year. Thai, Lao and Khmer versions do not agree on the naga's genealogy, and the Khmer foundation story is known mainly through later chronicles and Chinese records.

title: The Kinnari and the Hunter
source_ref: The Sudhana-Manohara tale in the Panyasa Jataka (Chiang Mai, c. 1450-1470); Thai Manora and Khmer Preah Sothon tellings; Borobudur reliefs
paragraphs: The kinnari are bird-women of Southeast Asian Buddhist and courtly art: human from the waist up, with wings, a tail and bird's feet. They live in forests and mountains, sing and dance, and are often paired with the male kinnara. In the Thai and Khmer tale, Manohara is the youngest of seven kinnari sisters who fly down from Mount Kailash to bathe in a forest pool.

A hunter, taught by a hermit, sets a magic noose around the pool where the sisters bathe. The others escape, but Manohara is caught. The hunter brings her to Prince Suthon, who frees her, falls in love with her and marries her. For a time she lives as a human queen, folding away her wings.

When Suthon is away at war, a courtier accuses Manohara of bringing misfortune and threatens her life. She puts on her wings and flies home, leaving a ring and directions for her husband. Suthon follows her for seven years, seven months and seven days, learns the language of animals from a hermit, and passes the kinnara king's tests: lifting a stone bench, shooting a bow, and picking Manohara out from her identical sisters.

He chooses her by the ring on her finger, and the couple is reunited. The tale is a swan-maiden story, a Buddhist jataka and a dance-drama all at once. Versions differ across Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Malaysia: the number of sisters, the hunter's role and the tests change. In southern Thailand the story is performed as Nora, a living tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.
notes: The tale survives in many versions. In the Panyasa Jataka Manohara is one of seven sisters and the prince is Sudhana; Thai tellings call him Phra Suthon and make the story a dance-drama, while Burmese versions have nine sisters and different tests. The number of sisters, the hunter's motive and the tests vary, and modern retellings often comment on the coercive premise of the capture and marriage.

title: The Buddha and the Naga
source_ref: Udana 2.1 (Mucalinda Sutta), Pali canon; Theravada Buddhist art of Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar
paragraphs: After his awakening, the Buddha sat in meditation for seven days under the Bodhi tree. Later he moved to the foot of the Mucalinda tree and sat there for another seven days. A great storm arose, with cold rain and wind. The naga king Mucalinda came out of his dwelling, coiled his body seven times around the Buddha, and spread his hood over him like a roof.

When the storm passed, Mucalinda released the Buddha, took the form of a young man and stood before him with joined hands. The Buddha praised the joy of a mind at peace, and the naga is remembered as a guardian of the teaching. In the Pali canon the episode shows the Buddha's mastery over the elements and the respect of the naga world for him.

Southeast Asian Buddhist art made the scene its own. In Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar the naga-prok image shows the Buddha seated under a great naga hood, often with the serpent's body coiled beneath him. The image appears in bronze, stone and wood, at temples and in household shrines, and it is one of the region's most recognisable Buddhist forms.

This is a Buddhist story, not a separate naga myth. It belongs to the Pali canon and to Theravada practice, and it explains why the naga is honoured as a protector of the Dhamma rather than feared as a monster. The naga of the Mekong and the naga who sheltered the Buddha belong to one cosmology; the same communities tell both stories in the same temples.
